sm: Matt Walsh discusses the conviction of Russell Brand on one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, and his sentence of nearly ten years in prison. Walsh calls Brand a degenerate who bears responsibility for his own fate, but argues the prosecution was a sham and a travesty of justice with more than enough reasonable doubt. He says the case was brought because Brand broke from the left during the COVID period and became a conservative commentator. He plays clips from the sentencing and from reporters hounding Brand's father, who suggested the verdict could be wrong, and objects to reporters asking what kind of man raised him.

Walsh says the case was tried in the media long before court, led by Channel 4 and the Times, so Brand could not have received an impartial jury. He compares it to the Cornell 7 case and says the burden of proof was not met. He then argues that rape cases in the US and UK are stacked against defendants: accusers are granted anonymity, which blocks investigation of their histories, and evidence of prior sexual behavior is largely barred even though, he says, it bears on credibility. He then begins going through the accusations, starting with a woman who said Brand raped her in a hotel room at a 1999 Labour Party conference. He notes there was no evidence beyond a photo showing they met, and Brand was acquitted.

Walsh continues with the acquittals. One was an attempted indecent assault claim from 2001 at MTV's London office, which the woman did not report until after the 2023 documentary. He then describes a 2004 Soho bar allegation, where the woman first said Brand tried to assault her and later said rape. The jury rejected the rape claim but convicted him of sexual assault for allegedly grabbing her breasts, which Walsh calls incoherent since she was found unreliable on one point. He adds that nobody in the crowded bar reportedly witnessed it.

Walsh argues that friends the woman called afterward are not independent corroboration, and that their accounts said only that Brand was pushy or aggressive, with no specifics until after the 2023 Channel 4 and Times documentary. He plays a clip from the documentary in which an anonymous woman called Alice alleges grooming as a minor, a claim that was never charged. He then turns to the most serious conviction, the 2009 rape charge. The woman said she consented to sex, but Brand removed the condom and had anal sex without consent. Walsh says it is nearly impossible to prove one act within a consensual encounter seventeen years later.

Walsh says the woman had a boyfriend yet voluntarily went backstage for a threesome with Brand after meeting him at a comedy show, which he says makes her less reliable as a narrator. He notes her father and friends told her she had been raped after hearing her account, and much of the trial rested on hearsay. She never went to police but visited a sexual health clinic for tests. He suggests she may have felt disgust at how Brand treated her and told friends she was a victim to cope, though he allows she could be telling the truth. He says a plausible alternative means the jury could not convict, and mentions Brand's phone contact label for her.

Walsh cites a Facebook message in which the accuser said she felt like an idiot, was young and stupid, and was probably as much to blame. He then discusses an uncharged 2012 Los Angeles allegation, which has text messages and a visit to a rape treatment center, but says it was about condom use, is time-barred, and is irrelevant to the convictions. He covers two other convictions: one for putting his head in a woman's groin after insisting on a massage in 2009, and one for kissing and groping a woman at a radio station in 2004 or 2005. He calls the documentary a political hit job that may have led women to invent memories, comparing it to the McMartin preschool panic.

Walsh says some women may have come forward for attention or because memory can change, and that the documentary only existed because Brand betrayed the left. He quotes the Guardian calling Brand a hero in 2014 and notes the New Statesman had him as guest editor. He says Brand turned on the left over COVID lockdowns and surveillance, and plays clips of his lockdown commentary. He says European elites would not tolerate this, so the documentary followed in 2023. He then compares Brand's ten-year sentence to shorter ones given in Britain to men convicted in grooming-gang cases, naming Muhammad Ali Sultan with seven years, Muhammad Yunus, Tanvir Ahmed and Muhammad Islam Choudhary.

Walsh compares Brand's sentence to a case in which a person named Katie Yowmans received five years and three months for fatally stabbing a man. He argues Brand got double the sentence of child rapists and murderers because he challenged the British government, and that the prosecution is a message to other commentators. He adds that Brand's behavior gave them ammunition, and that men who live in sexual chaos set themselves up to be destroyed, since the system will not let someone leave that life and become a public critic of it. He says a man can repent but the world is not merciful. He ends by mentioning that a film, Confession, premieres on Daily Wire the next day.
